title: London School of Economics
wiki_lead:
The London School of Economics and Political Science, commonly known as the London School of Economics (LSE),  is a public research university in London, England, and a member institution of the University of London. The school specialises in pure and applied social sciences.
Founded in 1895 by Fabian Society members Sidney Webb, Beatrice Webb, Graham Wallas and George Bernard Shaw, LSE joined the University of London in 1900 and offered its first degree programmes under the auspices of that university in 1901. In 2008, LSE began awarding degrees in its own name. LSE became a university in its own right within the University of London in 2022.
LSE is located in the London Borough of Camden and Westminster, Central London, near the boundary between Covent Garden and Holborn in the area historically known as Clare Market. As of 2023/24, LSE had under 13,000 students, with a majority enroled being postgraduate students and just under two thirds coming from outside the United Kingdom. The university has the sixth-largest endowment of any university in the UK and  it had an income of £548.2 million in 2024/25, of which £39.2 million was from research grants.
LSE is a member of the Russell Group, the Association of Commonwealth Universities and the European University Association, and is typically considered part of the "golden triangle" of research universities in the south east of England. The British Library of Political and Economic Science, commonly referred to as "LSE Library", is the main library of the university, and one of the largest libraries in the world devoted to the economic and social sciences.
Since 1990, the London School of Economics has educated 24 prime ministers or presidents, the second highest number of any university in the United Kingdom. Since the school's founding in 1895, over 40 world leaders, 21 Nobel laureates, two presidents of the European Commission and three presidents of the International Court of Justice have taught or studied at LSE.

History


Origins
The London School of Economics and Political Science was founded in 1895 by Beatrice and Sidney Webb, Graham Wallas and George Bernard Shaw initially funded by a bequest of £20,000 from the estate of Henry Hunt Hutchinson. Hutchinson, a lawyer and member of the Fabian Society, left the money in trust, to be put "towards advancing its [The Fabian Society's] objects in any way they [the trustees] deem advisable". The five trustees were Sidney Webb, Edward Pease, Constance Hutchinson, W. S. de Mattos and William Clark.
LSE records that the proposal to establish the school was conceived during a breakfast meeting on 4 August 1894, between the Webbs, Louis Flood, and George Bernard Shaw. The proposal was accepted by the trustees in February 1895 and LSE held its first classes in October of that year, in rooms at 9 John Street, Adelphi, in the City of Westminster.

grok_lead: The London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE) is a specialist public research university in central London, England, focused on the social sciences, including economics, politics, and sociology. Founded in 1895 by Fabian Society members Sidney Webb, Beatrice Webb, Graham Wallas, and George Bernard Shaw, it was established to provide rigorous scientific training in the analysis of industrial, economic, and political institutions, drawing on empirical evidence to inform social reform. LSE joined the federal University of London in 1900 and opened its doors to both men and women from inception, including international students. Over its history, LSE has achieved prominence through its research output and alumni, with 21 staff or students awarded Nobel Prizes, including 16 in Economic Sciences for contributions to fields like economic growth, institutions, and labor markets. Its faculty and graduates have advised governments and shaped policies worldwide, producing 24 heads of state or government since 1990, while maintaining a reputation for analytical rigor across ideological spectrumsâfrom Fabian origins to hosting free-market economists like Friedrich Hayek. Ranked as the top university in the UK for 2025 and 2026 by the Times and Sunday Times Good University Guide, LSE emphasizes evidence-based inquiry in a global student body exceeding 12,000. Despite these accomplishments, LSE has faced scrutiny for institutional decisions, such as accepting a Â£1.5 million donation from the Saif al-Islam Gaddafi Foundation in 2008, linked to Libya's regime, which an internal Woolf Inquiry deemed a "chapter of failures" involving ethical lapses and undue haste, leading to the 2011 resignation of director Howard Davies. This episode highlighted risks in engaging with authoritarian-linked funding, amid broader critiques of academic incentives prioritizing resources over scrutiny of donor credibility.
